content: The PENTA Foundation has provided funding for research, which was allocated to the recipient's institution without any personal financial benefit. The World Health Organization (WHO) Guideline Steering Group and the responsible technical officer reviewed the relevant information and deemed full participation in the process appropriate. Wendy Stevens received research funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and the Medical Research Council (MRC) for tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics, which was determined not to conflict with the guidelines. Consequently, full participation was allowed. The responsible technical officers evaluated all completed declarations of interest forms submitted by external contributors, including members of the External Review Group, to identify potential conflicts of interest. Each member of the External Review Group, including representatives from partner organizations such as the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and UNICEF, was required to complete and sign a declaration of interest form. Comments from the group were considered in light of any declared conflicts of interest. Details of these declarations and the management plan are documented in Web Annex A, with all forms securely stored electronically at the WHO Department of HIV for a minimum of 10 years. The document also provides detailed information on the toxicities and drug-drug interactions associated with antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, including first-, second-, and third-line therapies. Specific toxicities, risk factors, and management strategies are outlined for drugs such as abacavir (ABC), atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), zidovudine (AZT), dolutegravir (DTG), and others. For example, hypersensitivity reactions to ABC are linked to the presence of the HLA-B5701 gene, and its use is contraindicated in such cases. Similarly, ATV/r may cause electrocardiographic abnormalities and indirect hyperbilirubinemia, with management strategies tailored to individual risk factors. The guidelines also address the management of ARV drug interactions, particularly with medications such as rifampicin, anticonvulsants, and polyvalent cation-containing products. Recommendations include dose adjustments or substitutions to mitigate adverse effects and maintain therapeutic efficacy. Dosage recommendations for ARV drugs are provided for adults, adolescents, and children, including weight-based dosing for pediatric populations. Simplified dosing schedules for child-friendly formulations are emphasized, with a preference for fixed-dose combinations and dispersible tablets over oral liquids. Special considerations are outlined for neonates, preterm infants, and children with low birth weight, given their unique pharmacokinetic profiles and developmental immaturity. They also stress the need for national programs to verify the regulatory approval and quality of ARV formulations used in their settings. Research is ongoing to refine dosing recommendations for neonates and young children, with updates to be incorporated as new data and formulations become available. Finally, the document underscores the inclusion of integrase inhibitors, such as dolutegravir, as preferred options in updated ARV regimens. While dolutegravir is currently approved for children above certain age and weight thresholds, ongoing studies aim to expand its use to younger and smaller pediatric populations. Programs are encouraged to plan for the introduction of pediatric dolutegravir as simplified dosing schedules are confirmed.
